name: Independent on Sunday cryptic crossword No 1,845

entries.clue: Little steam engine in DC somebody uncoupled (8)

indicatorNotes.in: 'in' puts what stands before it inside what stands after, so the engine ends up between the two letters

blocks.note: the D of DC, left standing on its own
Ivor the Engine, the small Welsh steam engine of the children's cartoon
the C of DC spelt out the way it is said, CEE

annotation.surface: A little locomotive shunted about in Washington DC and left unhitched by somebody.
annotation.walkthrough: Ivor the Engine is a children's television steam engine from the Welsh valleys. The trap is reading DC as one thing: the two letters are handled separately, and the second is written out the way you say it.
annotation.definitionFit: A divorcee is somebody whose marriage has been dissolved — uncoupled in the domestic sense, not the railway one the surface offers.

entries.clue: Motown changes first two notes for popular opening song (7)

indicatorNotes.changes: 'changes' means swaps one thing for another, so the letters named next walk out and their replacement takes the place

blocks.note: Motown, the motor town, is Detroit
DETROIT opens with D and E, both notes of the scale
what comes in exchange is IN, meaning fashionable

annotation.surface: A record label reworking the first bars of a track to give it a chart-friendly opening.
annotation.walkthrough: Motown was Berry Gordy's Detroit label, named for the motor city, so the nickname hands over the city. An introit is the chant sung as a church service begins.
annotation.definitionFit: An introit is the psalm or antiphon sung while the priest approaches the altar, so it is literally the song that opens the service.

entries.clue: On bedding male friend's mother, complain to him? (9)

annotation.definitionNote: The definition describes the answer by his job instead of naming him, and the question mark flags that sideways approach; the answer is the noun for the man the phrase points at.

indicatorNotes.bedding: to bed something is to settle it down inside a surrounding material, so ON closes over everything that follows

blocks.note: the outer word, opened up to take the rest
m = male
a bud is a friend, and the apostrophe-s is read as a plain S
ma = mother

annotation.surface: Somebody has gone to bed with his male friend's mother, and you are invited to complain about it.
annotation.walkthrough: BUD for friend is American and worth knowing. The shape to spot is a two-letter word prised apart — ON becoming O…N — which is how nine letters come out of four short pieces.
annotation.definitionFit: An ombudsman is the official appointed to investigate grievances against a company or a government body, so he is precisely who you take a complaint to.

entries.clue: Well, I never put on security belt (6)

blocks.note: 'Cor!' is the British gasp of surprise that 'well, I never' spells out at length
to don a coat is to put it on

annotation.surface: A speaker protesting that they never once wore the safety belt.
annotation.walkthrough: The answer is shared between 4 and 23, three letters each. COR is the crossword's standard exclamation and turns up wherever a clue sounds astonished.
annotation.definitionFit: A cordon is the ring of police or troops thrown round a place to seal it off — a belt of security rather than one you buckle.

entries.clue: English cuckoo up tree is inspiration for musician (7)

indicatorNotes.cuckoo: 'cuckoo' means mad, and letters sent mad will not stay in the order they were given

blocks.note: e = English
anagram fodder, 6 letters
anagram indicator

annotation.surface: An English cuckoo calling from up a tree and firing up a passing musician.
annotation.walkthrough: Euterpe is one of the nine Muses, the one who presided over music, so 'inspiration' is literal: a muse is where the Greeks said it came from. The bird is scenery — cuckoo is here as an adjective.
annotation.definitionFit: Euterpe is the Muse of music and lyric poetry, the goddess a musician was supposed to be inspired by.

entries.clue: Give away money you put down shaft (6)

blocks.note: the money you put down on a horse is a bet
a shaft of light is a ray

annotation.surface: Handing over the money you staked and dropping it down a shaft.
annotation.walkthrough: Both halves are everyday words wearing other hats, the stake at the bookmaker's and the shaft of sunlight, and neither has anything to do with treachery.
annotation.definitionFit: To betray a secret is to give it away, the sense of letting something slip rather than the grander one of treason.

entries.clue: Unhappy about cutting best work, display temper (4,4,3)

indicatorNotes.cutting: something cutting into a word goes inside it, so the short pieces slice their way into BEST

blocks.note: the word BEST, taken whole before it is cut into
feeling low = unhappy
a book on beetles is a book about them
op, short for opus, is a composer's work

annotation.surface: An editor unhappy at having to cut the best piece of writing he has.
annotation.walkthrough: The surface sells 'cutting best work' as one act of editing, while the instruction is that two pieces cut into BEST itself. OP is the abbreviation printed on every concert programme.
annotation.definitionFit: To blow one's top is to lose your temper noisily, the picture being a lid flying off under pressure.

entries.clue: Decoratively hung ribbons used experimentally (10)

blocks.note: tapes are narrow ribbons of cloth
something tried has been used to see how it works

annotation.surface: Ribbons strung up as decoration and given a trial run.
annotation.walkthrough: A tapestried hall is hung with tapestries, the woven panels that covered cold stone walls. The answer divides between 7 and 21, five letters each.
annotation.definitionFit: Tapestried means hung with tapestry, so the decoration is in the word itself rather than in how it was put up.

entries.clue: Charge if aluminium boxes also sent to America (7)

indicatorNotes.boxes: to box something is to shut it in a container, so AL closes round the letters named after it

blocks.note: Al is the chemical symbol for aluminium
the cc line at the foot of a letter lists the people it was also sent to
USA = America

annotation.surface: A shipping charge that applies if the aluminium crates go to America as well.
annotation.walkthrough: Every noun is in disguise: the metal becomes its symbol, the boxes turn into an instruction, and the copy line off a memo supplies two letters.
annotation.definitionFit: An accusal is the noun from 'accuse', a charge levelled at somebody in the courtroom sense rather than a sum on an invoice.

entries.clue: Short pencil delivered at end of term unlikely to bend (8)

blocks.note: a pencil worn down to a stub
a baby delivered at the end of its term is born

annotation.surface: A worn-down pencil handed over on the last day of the school term.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Term' swaps school for pregnancy — a baby carried to term — and that switch is what hides the second half. The answer runs on into 24 across.
annotation.definitionFit: A stubborn person will not give way under pressure, and 'unlikely to bend' catches that refusal rather than any physical stiffness.

entries.clue: Time mushroom picker retired, in hindsight (10)

indicatorNotes.retired: someone retired has gone back, and these letters go back too, read from the far end

blocks.note: t = time
a cep is the fat edible mushroom the Italians call porcini
a sorter picks items out and puts them in their places

annotation.surface: It was time the mushroom picker gave up work, or so it looks now.
annotation.walkthrough: CEP is one of the crossword's two standard mushrooms. Everything is written backwards, which is why 'time' supplies the letter at the far end of the answer rather than the near one.
annotation.definitionFit: Retrospect is the backward look you take at an event once it is over, the same thing hindsight names.

entries.clue: So-so hurdler running around yard behind house, not so fast (4,4,6)

indicatorNotes.running around: letters running around are letters out of their places, and the yard gets caught up in the run
indicatorNotes.behind: what is behind the house comes after it, so HO leads and the jumbled letters follow

blocks.note: ho. is the estate agent's abbreviation of house
anagram fodder, 11 letters
y = yard, thrown in among the fodder
anagram indicator

annotation.surface: A mediocre hurdler doing laps of the yard behind a house.
annotation.walkthrough: Hurdles and horses sit so comfortably together that the racing word reads as scenery rather than as raw material. HO for house is the abbreviation off an estate agent's board.
annotation.definitionFit: 'Hold your horses' is what you say to somebody rushing at something, reining them in exactly as 'not so fast' does.

entries.clue: Public doshed out more than necessary (4,3,4)

indicatorNotes.out: 'out' is the sense in 'dished out' — scattered round the table, and the letters scatter with it

blocks.note: an overt threat is a public, undisguised one
anagram fodder, 6 letters
anagram indicator

annotation.surface: Cash dished out to the public more freely than it needed to be.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Doshed' is not a word, which is the tell that its letters are wanted and not its meaning. Dosh is British slang for money, so the surface still reads as a payout.
annotation.definitionFit: To pay over the odds is to pay above the going rate, the odds being the price a bookmaker would have quoted.

entries.clue: Rush from officially authorised drug (8)

blocks.note: a form officially authorised has been stamped
E is ecstasy

annotation.surface: The rush that comes off a drug somebody has officially approved.
annotation.walkthrough: Nothing in the clue mentions animals, and that is the disguise: 'rush' reads as the lift a drug gives before it turns out to mean a herd in flight.
annotation.definitionFit: A stampede is a sudden headlong rush of cattle or of people, which is the noun 'rush' straight.

entries.clue: Say, lie outrageously without anxiety (6)

indicatorNotes.outrageously: behaving outrageously is behaving without order, and the letters follow suit

blocks.note: anagram fodder, 6 letters
anagram indicator

annotation.surface: Somebody telling a shameless whopper without turning a hair.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Say' looks like the crossword's usual signal for an example coming, which is what keeps it hidden in the fodder. The comma after it is punctuation the setter is free to ignore.
annotation.definitionFit: To sleep easily is to sleep without anxiety; the adverb carries the untroubled sense as well as the effortless one.

entries.clue: That might be 26 sheep in odd places on farming land (9)

annotation.definitionNote: The definition sends you to 26 across, SUNDERED; 'might be' turns that past participle into the adjective for something it could be done to, which is what the answer is.

indicatorNotes.in odd places: letters in odd places are the ones standing first, third and fifth, so only every other letter is taken
indicatorNotes.on: in a down clue what is on something sits above it, so the letters from the sheep go on top of the land

blocks.note: the odd letters of SHEEP are S, E and P
arable land is land ploughed for crops

annotation.surface: Sheep dotted here and there across the ploughed fields.
annotation.walkthrough: The cross-reference means this one only falls once 26 across is in. Arable land is under crops rather than grass, which is why sheep standing about on it look wrong.
annotation.definitionFit: Something separable can be pulled apart — sundered, as 26 across puts it — so the definition is that answer turned into a possibility.

entries.clue: Hearing from Londoner, Bordeaux sweltering I suppose? (3,3)

indicatorNotes.Hearing from Londoner: 'hearing' asks for the sound rather than the spelling, and 'from Londoner' fixes whose accent you are to hear it in

blocks.note: Bordeaux is French wine country, so Bordeaux stands for wine; sweltering is hot; the Londoner drops the aitch, and the two words run together

annotation.surface: A Londoner remarking that the claret has gone warm.
annotation.walkthrough: Dropping the aitch is the whole mechanism — keep it and there is no sound to hear. Bordeaux stands in for wine the way Champagne stands in for fizz, the region named instead of the drink.
annotation.definitionFit: 'Why not?' is the shrug you give when agreeing to something you have no strong feelings about, which is what 'I suppose?' does.

entries.clue: American wit keeps papers in damp box (7)

indicatorNotes.keeps: to keep something is to hold on to it inside, so the wit shuts the papers away within itself

blocks.note: humor is the American spelling of humour
your ID is the papers you are asked to produce

annotation.surface: An American humorist keeping his papers in a box that has gone damp.
annotation.walkthrough: 'American' is there for the spelling, not for the man's passport. A humidor is kept deliberately moist so the cigars inside it never dry out.
annotation.definitionFit: A humidor is the lidded box a smoker keeps cigars in, held damp on purpose so they stay supple.

entries.clue: Potty US billionaire stores Tesla upright at the end of the drive? (8)

annotation.definition: upright at the end of the drive?

indicatorNotes.stores: to store something is to put it away inside, so the billionaire's name takes the potty in

blocks.note: Bill Gates, who founded Microsoft
a po is a chamber pot, the potty that used to live under the bed
the tesla, the SI unit of magnetic flux density, has the symbol T

annotation.surface: A crazy American billionaire keeping a Tesla at the end of his driveway.
annotation.walkthrough: Tesla points hard at Musk while the wordplay wants Gates, and the car turns out to be a unit of magnetic flux density named after the engineer. The question mark admits a gatepost is only one thing an upright there could be.
annotation.definitionFit: A gatepost is the upright the gate swings on, standing where a drive meets the road.

entries.clue: Some French people gossip about old pair in rubber (7)

blocks.note: to gas is to talk idly, so gas = gossip
c for circa, as in 'about 1900'
o = old
a rubber is a set of games at bridge, and its four players sit as two pairs, North-South and East-West

annotation.surface: Gossip going round about the old couple in the bridge rubber.
annotation.walkthrough: Gascons come from Gascony in south-west France; d'Artagnan was one. The last two letters are bridge, where players are named for the compass point they sit at.
annotation.definitionFit: Gascons are the people of Gascony in the south-west corner of France, so they are some of the French rather than all of them.

entries.clue: Son given bottle, stifling a curse (7)

indicatorNotes.stifling: to stifle something is to smother it before it gets out, so the letter named after it never reaches the word

blocks.note: s = son
bottle is British slang for nerve — 'he lost his bottle'
this A is the letter stifled out of COURAGE, leaving COURGE

annotation.surface: A son handed a bottle, biting back a swear word.
annotation.walkthrough: Bottle for nerve is British slang, and it is the word rather than the object the clue wants. A scourge was a whip long before it was a plague, which is how it came to mean an affliction.
annotation.definitionFit: A scourge is an affliction visited on people, so it matches curse in the sense of a blight rather than a swear word.

entries.clue: Female leader, Tories rampant with her our PM (6,8)

indicatorNotes.rampant: something rampant is running unchecked in every direction, which is what the letters do here

blocks.note: anagram fodder, 6 letters
fodder, 3 letters
fodder, 3 letters
fodder, 2 letters
anagram indicator

annotation.surface: Tories running wild alongside a woman prime minister of ours.
annotation.walkthrough: Everything after the first two words is fodder, fourteen letters of it, which is why the clue reads as smooth political comment. Rampant is heraldry's word for a beast reared up on its hind legs.
annotation.definitionFit: A Mother Superior is the nun who runs a convent, so the title is a woman in charge by definition.

entries.clue: See 7
Dickensian fellow with unopened red and corkscrew cross (5,5)

indicatorNotes.unopened: a word left unopened keeps everything except the letter that opens it, so RED starts one letter later

blocks.note: RED with its opening R taken off
to corkscrew through a hillside is to wind through it
a rood is the great cross set above the screen in an English church

annotation.surface: A fellow out of Dickens with an unopened red, a corkscrew and a cross expression.
annotation.walkthrough: Edwin Drood is the title character of the novel Dickens left unfinished when he died, so nobody knows what became of him. 'Unopened' looks like it belongs to the wine and is an instruction to the word RED.
annotation.definitionFit: Edwin Drood is the young man whose disappearance drives The Mystery of Edwin Drood, making him a Dickensian fellow by birth.

entries.clue: See 4
See 9
Puritanical types obscene in writing afterwards (6)

indicatorNotes.in: 'in' drops what comes before it inside what comes after, so the obscenity lands between the two letters

blocks.note: the PS is the bit written after a letter is already finished
a rude joke is an obscene one

annotation.surface: Somebody slipping something filthy into the postscript of a letter.
annotation.walkthrough: A rude word sits inside the very people who would object to it. PS splits into its two letters here, which is the only way a six-letter answer comes out of it.
annotation.definitionFit: A prude is shocked by anything to do with sex or the body, which is what puritanical means once it loses its capital P.

entries.clue: Split second subeditor's position? (8)

indicatorNotes.position: 'position' means the post somebody holds, so the job title is spelt out as the words it is built from

blocks.note: s = second
the sub- of subeditor means under
and its editor shortens to the usual ed

annotation.surface: A split second, and the position a subeditor holds on the paper.
annotation.walkthrough: A subeditor trims copy and writes the headlines, and the answer simply reads his title as the two words it is made of, an under-editor. 'Split second' is one phrase on the surface and two separate jobs underneath.
annotation.definitionFit: Sundered means forced apart, the past participle of 'sunder', which survives mostly in formal writing for things split in two.
